messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The accident happened on a Tuesday evening in late October, just as the sun was setting. Carlos was driving home from a rehearsal at the community theater where he taught Afro-Cuban dance, his body still humming with the rhythm of the rumba he had been demonstrating. A pickup truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan on the driver's side. The impact spun the car twice before it came to rest against a light pole. Carlos remembers the sound of tearing metal, the smell of gasoline, and the way his own voice sounded strange and distant when he tried to call out. He remembers the paramedic’s gloved hand on his shoulder, and how he flinched so hard he nearly hit his head on the stretcher rail. That flinch has never really stopped. Now, eight months later, he reacts with alarm when his wife, Elena, touches his arm to get his attention at the dinner table, and he has come to believe that his body no longer belongs to him in the way it once did.

Carlos cannot put the event into words. When his doctor asked him to describe what happened, he found himself mute, his throat tight, the images flooding back without language. What comes to him instead are sounds: the screech of tires, the low groan of twisting metal, the sharp pop of the airbag deploying. These auditory fragments rise up without warning, often in the middle of a dance class when a student’s sneaker squeaks against the floor or when the theater door slams shut. Each time they surface, he is flooded with a shame so acute it feels physical—a hot, crawling sensation under his skin. He has come to believe that the accident happened to him because of the sort of person he is: careless, distracted, someone who deserved to be punished. This conviction has taken root in him like a splinter he cannot remove. He is certain that he can never feel normal emotions again, that something essential inside him has been permanently shattered, and that no matter how carefully he lives, bad things will keep finding him because he is fundamentally the kind of person they happen to.

Because Carlos is convinced that catastrophe is always waiting, he has begun to scan for exits as soon as he enters any room or building. He does it automatically now—a quick, practiced sweep of the eyes that locates every door, every window, every possible escape route. The habit has become so ingrained that he cannot stop it, and the more he scans, the more vividly the memory of the crash returns: the blind panic of being trapped, the metal folding in around him, the certainty that he was about to die. Each memory reinforces his belief that he is helpless, that his character is flawed, that the world is a place where the next disaster is simply a matter of time. This loop tightens daily.

To manage the constant threat, Carlos has developed strategies that he knows, on some level, are not helping. He suppresses his thoughts about the trauma with tremendous effort, pushing them down the moment they surface, but the suppression itself seems to make the memories return more forcefully later, often as unbidden sounds or images that leave him disoriented and ashamed. He has also started staying up until very late, sometimes until three or four in the morning, because the hours before dawn feel safer—quieter, emptier, less likely to surprise him. The sleep deprivation leaves him exhausted and emotionally brittle, which in turn deepens his conviction that he is broken beyond repair. In the worst moments, he deliberately tries to leave his body, to blank out, to float somewhere above himself where the fear cannot reach him. But dissociation only fragments his memory further, making it harder to integrate what happened, and leaving him feeling more alienated from himself and from the life he used to lead.

The consequences have been concrete. Carlos has stopped teaching the advanced class because the dance studio has no back exit, only the single front door, and he cannot bear the trapped feeling that descends the moment he walks in. He now teaches only private lessons in a rented hall with four exits, and his income has dropped by nearly half. Elena has noticed that he no longer dances at home, that he flinches from her touch, that he spends his evenings staring at the ceiling instead of sleeping beside her. She asked him last week if he was angry with her, and he could not find the words to explain that he is not angry—he is terrified, and ashamed of being terrified, and convinced that he is no longer the man she married.

What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a moment in the grocery store last Tuesday. A child dropped a jar of pasta sauce, and the sound of glass shattering sent him to his knees in the aisle, his hands over his ears, his heart slamming against his ribs. A stranger helped him up. He could not stop apologizing. He is afraid that next time, he will not be able to get back up at all. He is hoping, more than he can say, that someone can help him find a way back into his own body, into his own life, before the man he used to be disappears entirely.
